summary:
Risaralda department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to state services rests on court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing the attack on Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia; she was assaulted in broad daylight, the assault was filmed, and she died the following afternoon at three o'clock. No one had been arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised and comes from armed groups. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she fled at night after hiding for a week, and "social cleansing" flyers circulated on the streets and by WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Earlier fatal attacks include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented in national reporting occurs within Colombia's decades-long civil conflict, and reporting describes the killing of queer Colombians after the Millerey case as calculated brutality rather than opportunistic crime. Armed groups that never demobilised under the 2016 peace agreement run the flyer campaigns, which converts homophobic and transphobic messaging into an operational threat with named targets and stated deadlines.

Employment discrimination is a structural feature of the national picture rather than an incidental one: trans women are reported as limited mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which shapes where they are visible and how exposed they are to street violence. Risaralda sits in a departmental region where this pattern of economic exclusion and armed-group activity is documented elsewhere in the country, so the absence of a Risaralda-specific incident report should not be read as an absence of the underlying conditions.

Colombia's legal position compares favourably with most of Latin America on paper: notary-based marker change, constitutional recognition of self-identification dating from 1993, marriage equality, adoption rights and official trans and non-binary document markers. The gap identified by the UN Independent Expert in May 2025 is between that institutional record and daily lived experience, a formulation that applies to Risaralda as to the cities covered by the mission.
localsOnly:
Residents of Risaralda change the sex marker on their cédula and other government identification by signing a document before a notary, a procedure available nationally since the June 2015 rule change; no judicial order, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment is required, and the 1993 Constitutional Court jurisprudence removes any surgical requirement.

Colombian identification documents have carried official "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, so residents can hold documents that record gender identity directly rather than only a binary sex entry.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree binds government institutions in Risaralda on LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and for victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree extends guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Residents in state custody are covered by the 2011 ruling on personal presentation and by subsequent jurisprudence on the treatment of trans detainees.

Residents who entered a same-sex marriage abroad may have it registered by any notary or registrar under the National Registry memo, and same-sex spouses hold the same visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presentation of a stamped marriage certificate and identification.

Trans residents face documented economic limits: national reporting records hairdressing and sex work as the main occupations available, and where armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns operate, trans women have been given deadlines to leave towns or be killed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a Risaralda-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. The department's record is built from the national framework and from documented incidents in Antioquia, Caquetá and Guajira; whether Risaralda police, prosecutors or courts have handled a trans-specific case, and how local authorities apply the 2016 and 2018 decrees, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The status of a comprehensive national statute on gender identity and against discrimination is not documented in the available material; any claim that such a bill is pending, stalled or enacted cannot be verified from these sources.

Death tolls for 2023 appear in two forms in the inventory, "more than 40" and "41" transgender women killed, which are consistent but not reconciled to a single official count. The 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office cover January to May 2025 and are not broken down by gender identity.

Whether the Virgilio Barco or other Risaralda health providers offer trans-related care, and whether local notaries in Pereira, Dosquebradas or La Virginia have processed marker changes without obstruction, is not addressed by any source supplied.
